# Research question

The larger project asks how predictable human lives are. Its first tractable
task is Dr. Jason Jeffrey Jones' [Predict Future Selves
challenge](https://github.com/jasonjeffreyjones/predict-future-selves): predict
a later self-authored self-description from an earlier self-authored
self-description.

This is an ipseological prediction task. A bio is *personally expressed
identity*: text an individual publishes for the purpose of describing themself.
Its words, hashtags, abbreviations, and emoji may serve as identity signifiers.
The target is later personally expressed identity—not a latent "true self" and
not a complete life outcome.

# What the prior demonstration establishes

The presentation describes OPTS Mark 1, an earlier oracle trained with 112,541
longitudinal pairs of United States Twitter bios from 2015 and 2020. Each row
contained an `Early_Bio` and a `Later_Bio` for the same user. The demonstration
showed that an oracle could identify broad change patterns and, when directly
prompted, retrieve useful signifier-level regularities. It also produced
anodyne conclusions and left the author "disappointed but intrigued."

Those findings motivate the new challenge, but they do not specify its current
participant instructions, prediction cases, allowed resources, or scoring
rule. The older demonstration therefore cannot substitute for the challenge
README.

# Participant protocol

The following procedure is fixed for the next iteration unless the challenge
README requires a different procedure.

1. Retrieve and archive the challenge README and all supplied participant
   files. Record the repository commit identifier and SHA-256 hashes of input
   files.
2. Read the complete instructions before examining any labels or answers.
3. Preserve every supplied bio exactly as given. Use normalized or tokenized
   representations only for supplemental analysis, never as replacements for
   the original text.
4. Keep any held-out later bios unavailable until all predictions are frozen.
5. Produce the required prediction artifact exactly once, then save it before
   evaluation.
6. Apply the challenge's official scoring procedure. If the instructions allow
   additional analysis, compare the participant result with at least a
   copy-the-earlier-bio baseline and any official baseline.
7. Report all cases and metrics, including failures; do not select only
   favorable examples.

This protocol protects the main result from answer leakage and preserves a
clear distinction between a genuine forecast and a post-outcome reconstruction.
